name: Number Line Navigator
topics_techniques_covered: number_sense_magnitude
number-line estimation: locate a target number on a bounded line
place a point or fraction at the correct location on a number line
interpret the value of a point marked on a number line
implicit ordering / magnitude comparison
one_liner: The child slides a marker to where a target number, fraction, or point belongs on a number line and releases to lock it in.
interaction: A horizontal number line is shown with labeled endpoints (sometimes one interior anchor). A target (numeral, fraction, pictured quantity, or a 'read this point' prompt) appears above. The child drags a glowing marker along the line and releases; the release position is the answer. For read-the-point variants the child instead taps one of 3-4 candidate values. Submission = release of the drag (auto-commit) with a ~1.5s undo/redrag window, plus a Lock button to confirm early.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<8s): a translucent hand grabs the marker, glides it to a lit target zone under the numeral 5 on a 0-10 line, and releases with a snap and chime; the target then changes and the hand repeats once. One unscored warm-up asks the child to place 2 on a 0-10 line with a wide green success band and gentle nudge arrows, so the drag-and-release mechanic is obvious with zero text.

learning_science.principle: Spatial-numeric mapping / mental number line
learning_science.why: Number-line estimation accuracy (linear vs logarithmic placement) is one of the most robust behavioral predictors of broad math achievement and reveals the precision of a child's internal magnitude representation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score continuous placement error (percent absolute error), not just right/wrong, and shift endpoints and scale to probe the linearity of the child's representation.
learning_science.source: Siegler & Opfer (2003), 'The development of numerical estimation: Evidence for multiple representations of numerical quantity', Psychological Science 14(3):237-243.

learning_science.principle: Concreteness fading
learning_science.why: Beginning with a concrete, manipulable representation and fading toward symbolic form supports transfer and lets young children reason about magnitude before mastering symbols.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses a picture counting track; older bands fade to bare labeled lines with fractions, decimals, and negatives using the same drag mechanic throughout.
learning_science.source: Fyfe, McNeil, Son & Goldstone (2014), 'Concreteness fading in mathematics and science instruction', Educational Psychology Review 26:9-25.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Placement error (percent absolute error)
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Continuous placement error turns a single number-line item into a fine-grained latent-magnitude signal; small, consistent PAE at hard scales (fractions, wide ranges) separates top reasoners far better than dichotomous accuracy and avoids ceiling.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Record released position, convert to a value, compute absolute(placed - target) / line-range as a percent per item; also fit the child's placement curve (linear vs log R^2).
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=10-15 placements spanning the scale for a stable PAE and linearity estimate.

tail_precision_rationale: PAE plus placement-curve linearity give a continuous ability index that keeps resolving differences after accuracy saturates; first-action latency and revision count separate reflective, confident placers (plan then commit) from guess-and-adjust behavior at the same accuracy, adding process variance exactly where gifted candidates cluster.
age_rationale: Drag-and-release on a large line is within K-1 motor range given a wide success tolerance; tolerance tightens and content shifts (0-10 counting to 0-100/0-1000, then fractions/decimals/negatives, then proportional scales) rather than changing the interaction, so one shell spans all bands. Reading load is near-zero (numerals and points).

adaptive.content_range: counting and magnitude (0-10) through fraction, decimal, and negative placement and proportional scaling (6-8); the interactive line is the sponsor's example of one shell spanning a huge content range without notation.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: scale/range, tolerance-band width, target type (whole/fraction/decimal/negative), presence or absence of interior anchors, hidden intermediate ticks, read-the-point vs place-the-point, and non-integer endpoints (e.g., 0 to 3/4).
adaptive.notes: Endpoints and targets are sampled programmatically; PAE thresholding drives adaptive escalation of scale difficulty.

engagement_hook: A 'lock it in' snap with a rising chime and a shrinking bullseye that rewards precision, so it feels like calibrating a dial rather than answering a math question.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor precision on tight tolerances (mitigate with age-scaled band widths and a redrag window); touch vs mouse pointer resolution (normalize tolerance to device); tick-counting shortcuts (sometimes hide intermediate ticks); ensure color-independent success cues.

name: Magnitude Duel
topics_techniques_covered: quantitative_comparison: greater / less / equal / cannot be determined
approximate number system dot-comparison: choose the array with more dots
symbolic magnitude comparison: choose the larger of two numbers
compare or order numbers, fractions, or decimals
one_liner: Two quantities flash side by side and the child quickly taps the side that is greater, or taps 'equal' or 'can't tell'.
interaction: Two panels appear (dot arrays, numerals, fractions, or short expressions). The child taps the larger panel; a center EQUAL button and, for older bands, a CAN'T TELL button handle ties and indeterminate cases. Response = single tap (no drag). Non-symbolic arrays are briefly shown then masked to force approximate comparison; symbolic items stay visible. A streak/combo builds on fast-and-correct taps and breaks on a wrong tap.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<7s): two clusters of fish appear, the hand taps the clearly-more side, a green pulse and points pop; it repeats once with numerals. One unscored warm-up uses an easy 2-vs-8 dot comparison so the tap-the-bigger rule is obvious without words.

learning_science.principle: Approximate Number System (ANS) acuity
learning_science.why: Non-symbolic magnitude discrimination acuity (the Weber fraction) is measurable pre-symbolically and correlates with current and future formal math achievement, letting young or low-literacy children demonstrate quantitative ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include flashed-then-masked dot arrays with an adaptive ratio and estimate the ratio at which the child crosses a threshold accuracy (the Weber fraction).
learning_science.source: Halberda, Mazzocco & Feigenson (2008), 'Individual differences in non-verbal number acuity correlate with maths achievement', Nature 455:665-668.

learning_science.principle: Worst-performance rule / RT consistency
learning_science.why: In speeded comparison, response consistency (low variability) and the slowest responses are more diagnostic of ability than peak speed; rewarding raw speed would be coachable and construct-irrelevant.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log the full RT distribution and credit accuracy-held speed via a speed-accuracy model; surface RT variability and lapses rather than the fastest tap.
learning_science.source: Coyle (2003), 'A review of the worst performance rule', Intelligence 31(6):567-587.

new_measurements_proposed.name: ANS acuity (Weber fraction)
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Estimates the finest numerical ratio a child can reliably discriminate; a less-coachable, low-literacy tail signal that keeps separating children when symbolic items would floor or ceiling, especially in K-1.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Adaptively vary the ratio of the two non-symbolic arrays (staircase), fit a psychometric function to accuracy-by-ratio, and report the Weber fraction w and its standard error.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=30-40 non-symbolic trials spanning ratios ~1.1 to 2.5 for a stable w.

tail_precision_rationale: Pairing a stable speed-accuracy operating point with RT variability and lapse rate (worst-performance) yields a less-coachable fluency index; the adaptive Weber fraction extends discrimination below the floor of symbolic items, so even children who ceiling on symbolic comparison remain separable by non-symbolic acuity.
age_rationale: Single-tap choice is the lowest motor demand of any type, suitable from K-1. Content escalates from dot arrays (no symbols) to numerals, then fractions/decimals, then expressions with cannot-be-determined logic (6-8); the tap interaction never changes and reading load stays minimal.

adaptive.content_range: non-symbolic subitizing/ANS (K-1) through fraction/decimal ordering and indeterminate symbolic comparison with unknowns (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: array ratio (Weber), symbolic vs non-symbolic, numeral magnitude/format (whole/fraction/decimal/negative), inclusion of equal / cannot-be-determined, exposure duration and masking, and size-vs-number congruency.
adaptive.notes: Trivially cloneable via numeric templates and array generators; a staircase on ratio/difficulty gives per-child adaptation.

engagement_hook: A fast arcade 'duel' with a combo meter: quick correct calls build a streak and a bad call breaks it, so it feels like a reflex game while covertly titrating magnitude acuity.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Speed pressure can induce impulsive fast-wrong responding (credit only accuracy-held speed; never reward raw speed); visual density/size can confound number (control dot area and include size-number-incongruent trials); keep equal and can't-tell buttons equally reachable to avoid position bias.

name: Number Series Stepping Stones
topics_techniques_covered: number_series: infer the rule of a number sequence and supply the next term
determine the missing number in a sequence
continue an early pictorial pattern or quantity sequence
pattern_completion: extend a repeating or growing pattern and state the rule
one_liner: A path of stepping stones shows a number sequence with one stone blank; the child works out the rule and sets the missing or next number.
interaction: A row of stones displays a sequence (pictures/dots for K-1, numerals for older). One stone is blank (next-term at the end or an interior missing term). The child sets the value by (a) tapping one of 4 candidate stones, or (b) using +/- steppers or a small keypad to dial the exact number, then taps the blank stone to place it. Submission = place/confirm. An optional 'show one more example' scaffold reveals a parallel worked series and is logged.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): stones read 2, 4, 6, ?; the hand hops along the stones showing the +2 gap as a glowing arc between each, then drops an 8 onto the blank stone with a splash; it repeats once with 1, 2, 3, ?. Unscored warm-up: 5, 6, 7, ? with candidate stones, so continue-the-pattern self-teaches wordlessly.

learning_science.principle: Inductive / relational reasoning (rule induction)
learning_science.why: Number-series completion is a classic marker of fluid and quantitative reasoning: the solver must induce a generating rule and project it, tapping relational reasoning strongly tied to general ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Design difficulty and distractors around rule type (constant difference, multiplicative, alternating, second-difference) and log error type to reveal partial rule induction.
learning_science.source: Holzman, Pellegrino & Glaser (1983), 'Cognitive variables in series completion', Journal of Educational Psychology 75(4):603-618.

learning_science.principle: Relational complexity limits reasoning by development
learning_science.why: Younger children handle adjacent/perceptual relations while older children manage higher-order relations; one series shell can span this by adjusting relational complexity.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses pictorial +1 growth (perceptual), older bands use multi-operation and second-order-difference rules (relational), with the same placement interaction.
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), 'Processing capacity defined by relational complexity', Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6):803-831.

tail_precision_rationale: Adaptive escalation of relational complexity yields M-DIFFREACH (the hardest rule the child cracks), the sharpest single tail statistic; error-type tagging (off-by-one vs wrong-operation vs additive-when-multiplicative) distinguishes near-miss latent ability from genuine rule failure, refining placement right at the cut.
age_rationale: K-1 uses pictorial/quantity growth with candidate stones (recognition, low motor and reading); 2-3 and up add steppers/keypad for exact entry; 6-8 use multiplicative, alternating, and second-difference rules. The stepping-stone placement is constant; only rule complexity and entry mode scale.

adaptive.content_range: count-on pictorial series (K-1) through geometric, alternating, and second-difference numeric series (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: rule type (additive/multiplicative/alternating/polynomial), step size, position of the blank (next vs interior), candidate vs free entry, number magnitude, and two interleaved rules.
adaptive.notes: Series generated from parameterized rule families; near-miss distractors auto-derived (off-by-step, wrong-operation).

engagement_hook: Hopping a character across stones to 'complete the bridge': placing the right number extends the path with a bounce, turning rule-finding into building a route forward.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Keypad/stepper entry adds motor and numeral-formation load (offer candidate-tap mode for young or motor-limited children); ensure distractors are not guessable by position; require no reading; cap digits so handwriting/working memory is not the bottleneck.

name: Build-a-Number Blocks
topics_techniques_covered: decompose a multi-digit number by place value and reason about its structure
place_value / base-ten composition and regrouping
number_properties_reasoning: even/odd, factors, or creating the largest result
number_sense_magnitude; numeration: identify, compare, and represent numbers
one_liner: The child composes a target quantity by dragging base-ten blocks (or ten-frame dots) into a workspace, regrouping units into tens as needed.
interaction: A target is shown (a numeral, a pictured/audio quantity, or a goal like 'make the largest number' or 'make an even number over 50'). The child drags unit, ten, hundred, and thousand blocks (K-1: dots into ten-frames) into bins while a live total updates. Ten units can be tapped to regroup into a ten and vice-versa. Submission = Done when the total matches or best meets the goal. A decompose variant asks the child to split a given number into place-value parts.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): target 13; the hand drags one ten-rod and three unit-cubes into the tray as the counter climbs 10, 11, 12, 13 and locks green; then it taps ten loose cubes to snap them into a rod (regrouping) once. Unscored warm-up: make 5 with unit cubes. No words needed.

learning_science.principle: Place-value / base-ten structure understanding
learning_science.why: Flexible composition, decomposition, and regrouping of multi-digit numbers is foundational number sense predicting later arithmetic and rational-number learning; manipulatives externalize the base-ten structure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require genuine regrouping (10 units to 1 ten) and log whether the child composes efficiently or by brute single-unit counting, capturing structural understanding beyond the final total.
learning_science.source: Fuson (1990), 'Conceptual structures for multidigit numbers', Cognition and Instruction 7(4):343-403.

learning_science.principle: Enactive-iconic-symbolic representation (Bruner)
learning_science.why: Acting on concrete objects supports magnitude and place-value reasoning before symbolic fluency, lowering the notation barrier for young or struggling children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Blocks are draggable manipulatives with a live symbolic counter that links enactive action to the symbol; K-1 uses ten-frames while older bands fade to place-value bins with decimals.
learning_science.source: Bruner (1966), 'Toward a Theory of Instruction', Harvard University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Efficiency-vs-optimal and the move path expose strategy: building 137 as 1 hundred + 3 tens + 7 units (place-value chunking) versus 137 loose units reveals structural mastery invisible in a right/wrong total; regrouping moves and revisions distinguish fluent, planful builders from trial-and-error at the tail.
age_rationale: Dragging blocks into bins is K-1 feasible with large targets and snap-to-bin. Content scales from ten-frames/units (K-1) to tens and ones (2-3), hundreds/thousands with regrouping (4-5), and decimals plus 'largest-number' and even/odd/factor goals (6-8). The interaction (drag + regroup-tap + Done) is constant.

adaptive.content_range: count/compose to 10 via ten-frames (K-1) through multi-digit regrouping, decimals, and number-property optimization goals such as 'largest even number from these digits' (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: target magnitude, number of place values, forced regrouping, decompose vs compose, goal type (exact match vs constraint optimization: largest/even/factor), decimal places, and limited block inventory.
adaptive.notes: Targets and inventories generated numerically; optimal solution known for M-EFF; constraint goals cover number_properties_reasoning.

engagement_hook: A tactile stacking-blocks sandbox where ten cubes snap into a rod with a click; building the number feels like play and the live counter makes progress visible and satisfying.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Fine-motor drag load (large blocks, snap-to-target, generous hit areas); brute-force counting instead of place-value reasoning (capture via M-EFF/M-PATH rather than penalizing outright); avoid reading via numeral/picture/audio targets; limit inventory clutter to reduce visual search load.

name: Balance Beam Equivalence
topics_techniques_covered: balance_equivalence: choose the weight(s) that keep a balance scale in equilibrium (Figure Weights)
number_sentence_building: enter values to balance both sides of an equation
mathematical-equivalence items (meaning of the equal sign, e.g. 3+4=_+5)
pre-algebraic reasoning without notation
one_liner: The child adds or removes weights (or numbers) on a pan balance to make both sides equal, discovering the value that keeps the beam level.
interaction: A pan balance tilts based on the true total on each pan. Pre-loaded weights, shapes, or numbers sit on each side; the child drags weights onto a pan or dials a value into an empty slot until the beam levels. The beam animates tilt in real time (the heavier side drops). Submission = Lock when level, or place the required missing weight. A Figure-Weights variant gives equivalences and asks which weight will balance the target.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the left pan shows 3 and the right shows 1, so the beam tilts left; the hand drags a 2 onto the right pan and the beam swings level with a settle and green glow; it repeats once. Unscored warm-up: one apple vs an empty pan, drag one apple to balance. The tilt makes 'make it level = make it equal' obvious with no words.

learning_science.principle: Relational understanding of the equal sign
learning_science.why: Many children hold an operational ('the answer comes next') view of '='; a relational view (both sides the same amount) uniquely predicts later algebra success, and a balance makes equivalence perceptual.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use non-canonical equivalence (e.g., 3+4 = _+5) on the pans so only relational reasoners succeed, and log operational-error signatures such as placing the running total in the blank.
learning_science.source: McNeil & Alibali (2005), 'Why won't you change your mind? Knowledge of operational patterns hinders learning and performance on equations', Child Development 76(4):883-899.

learning_science.principle: Balance-scale rule development (Siegler)
learning_science.why: Children progress through identifiable rules (weight-only, then distance, then integrated) on balance tasks, so the balance is a validated probe of reasoning level that scales from concrete to proportional/torque reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer weight-only balancing for young bands and distance/torque (arm-length) balancing for older bands to probe higher rule levels within one shell.
learning_science.source: Siegler (1976), 'Three aspects of cognitive development', Cognitive Psychology 8(4):481-520.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Relational-vs-operational equivalence signature
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Flags whether a child treats '=' relationally (balances both sides) or operationally (dumps a running total), a research-backed early separator of algebra-ready reasoning that dichotomous accuracy hides; concentrates information exactly where pre-algebraic talent emerges.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: On non-canonical equivalence items, classify the child's first substantive placement/entry against known operational-error targets vs the relational solution, and record whether they self-correct.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=4-6 non-canonical equivalence items to reliably classify the child's dominant strategy.

tail_precision_rationale: Real-time tilt turns solving into a guided search, so efficiency and exploration reveal whether the child computes the needed value directly (few, targeted moves) or hunts by trial. M-EQREL captures the relational/operational distinction that specifically forecasts algebra readiness, giving a qualitative tail separator beyond correctness.
age_rationale: Treating the beam as an equivalence relation (both sides must match a total) is the construct of interest and is beyond most K-1 children as a reasoning task, so K-1 is excluded to stay honest. 2-3 balance small whole-number totals; 4-5 add missing-addend and multi-weight cases; 6-8 add distance/torque and non-integer/ratio balancing. The drag/dial interaction suits grade 2 and up.

adaptive.content_range: concrete whole-number balancing (2-3) through missing-addend equivalence, multi-term sums, and distance/torque proportional balancing that encodes linear relationships without notation (6-8), a shell reaching pre-algebra/algebra reasoning.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of weights/terms, canonical vs non-canonical equivalence, missing-addend vs free-balance, weight-only vs distance/torque, integer vs fractional weights, and number of unknown slots.
adaptive.notes: Pan contents generated from equivalence templates; the torque variant introduces multiplicative reasoning; optimal move count known for M-EFF.

engagement_hook: A physically satisfying wobble-and-settle: the beam swings and teeters as weights land, so getting it perfectly level delivers immediate, game-like physical feedback.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Drag motor load (snap-to-pan, large weights); pure trial-and-error using the tilt cue (capture strategy via M-PATH/M-EFF and include commit-blind items for tail separation); avoid text via shapes/numerals; ensure tilt is readable without relying on color.

name: Function Machine
topics_techniques_covered: pattern_completion: 'number machine' input-output task, infer the transformation rule and give the output
generalize a growing figural-number pattern to the nth case and justify the relationship
pre-algebraic functional thinking
arithmetic_reasoning
one_liner: The child feeds numbers into a machine, watches inputs turn into outputs, infers the hidden rule, and predicts the output for a new input or assembles the rule.
interaction: A cartoon machine shows an input hopper and an output chute with a visible table of in-to-out examples (e.g., 2->5, 3->7, 4->9). The child may drag a limited number of test numbers into the hopper to see outputs (free probes), then answers the scored prompt: dial/tap the output for a new input, OR assemble the rule from operation tiles (e.g., [x2][+1]). Submission = confirm answer or rule. The free-probe count and choices are logged.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the machine shows 1->3 and 2->4; the hand drops a 3 in the hopper and a 5 pops out the chute (the +2 shown as two glowing dots added); then the hand dials 5 for input 4 correctly. Unscored warm-up: a +1 machine (1->2, 2->3, input 5 -> ?). The visible cause-effect self-teaches the infer-the-rule idea.

learning_science.principle: Functional thinking / early algebra
learning_science.why: Input-output 'function machine' reasoning develops the covariation and generalization at the heart of algebra, and children can reason functionally well before formal notation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer both 'predict the output' and 'build the rule from operation tiles' so children can express a general rule without algebraic symbols, escalating to two-step and nth-term generalization.
learning_science.source: Blanton & Kaput (2011), 'Functional thinking as a route into algebra in the elementary grades', in Early Algebraization (Springer), pp. 5-23.

learning_science.principle: Hypothesis testing / self-directed evidence sampling
learning_science.why: Letting the child probe inputs turns rule induction into active hypothesis testing; the efficiency and informativeness of chosen probes indexes scientific reasoning and separates systematic from random explorers.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Give a small budget of free test-inputs and log which probes the child chooses and how many before committing (informative vs redundant probing).
learning_science.source: Klahr & Dunbar (1988), 'Dual space search during scientific reasoning', Cognitive Science 12(1):1-48.

tail_precision_rationale: Probe efficiency (how few and how informative the test-inputs before a correct rule) is a strong strategy separator: gifted reasoners induce two-step rules from minimal evidence. M-DIFFREACH over one-step, two-step, and nth-term rules pinpoints the ceiling, and hint-free solving at high difficulty is stronger tail evidence.
age_rationale: Holding an input-output relation in mind and generalizing suits grade 2 and up with single-step additive rules; 4-5 adds multiplicative and two-step rules; 6-8 adds nth-term generalization and rule-building from tiles. The machine metaphor and drag/dial answer are constant. K-1 is excluded because rule induction over symbols exceeds typical readiness.

adaptive.content_range: single-step additive machines (2-3) through two-step linear rules and nth-term generalization that is algebra reasoning without notation (6-8), one shell spanning pattern to pre-algebra.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: rule arity (one/two-step), operation set (+,-,x,divide), number size, predict-output vs build-rule, number of visible examples, free-probe budget, and near vs far transfer (next term vs 10th/nth term).
adaptive.notes: Rules sampled from parametric families; distractors from common mis-rules (one step applied only, swapped operations).

engagement_hook: A whirring contraption that visibly transforms numbers; dropping test numbers to 'crack the machine's secret' turns algebra into a detective and tinkering game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Working-memory load from tracking examples (keep the example table visible); no reading required (numerals + iconic operation tiles); guessing on predict-output (mitigate with build-the-rule items and probe logging); cap arithmetic size so computation is not the reasoning bottleneck.

name: Number Analogy & Matrix
topics_techniques_covered: number_analogies: infer the quantitative relation in a 2x2 and complete it
numeric_matrix: find the missing number that satisfies a matrix of relations
quantitative_reasoning_mixed: verbal and nonverbal number problems and patterns
relational reasoning across rows and columns
one_liner: The child finds the quantitative relationship linking numbers in a 2x2 pair (or 3x3 grid) and supplies the missing number that fits the same relation.
interaction: A 2x2 (A:B :: C:?) or a 3x3 grid of numbers is shown with one cell blank. The child determines the relation across and/or down and answers by tapping one of 4 candidate numbers or dialing the value on a keypad, then confirms. For the matrix both the row and column relations must hold. Submission = confirm. A 'peek' scaffold can reveal the row relation once and is logged.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): 2:4 :: 3:? with a glowing 'x2' arrow drawn from 2 to 4; the same arrow then slides under 3 and the hand taps 6. Unscored warm-up: 1:2 :: 5:? with the mapping arrow shown. The animated relation-arrow teaches 'find what turns the top pair into each other, then apply it' without words.

learning_science.principle: Analogical reasoning (structure mapping)
learning_science.why: Analogies require mapping a relation from a source to a target rather than matching surface features; relational (vs attributional) responding marks higher reasoning and emerges with a relational shift in development.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Build distractors that are attractive on surface or additive grounds but wrong on the intended relation, so only true relational mappers succeed, and tag which relation each error implies.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), 'Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy', Cognitive Science 7(2):155-170.

learning_science.principle: Multiplicative relations develop later than additive
learning_science.why: Children default to additive relations before multiplicative ones; a number analogy readable either way separates children who access the multiplicative structure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include items where an additive misread yields a specific logged wrong answer, isolating additive-vs-multiplicative reasoning at the tail.
learning_science.source: Vergnaud (1983), 'Multiplicative structures', in Lesh & Landau (eds.), Acquisition of Mathematics Concepts and Processes (Academic Press), pp. 127-174.

tail_precision_rationale: Error-type tagging separates additive misreads from random error and pinpoints latent multiplicative reasoners; cross-item consistency on matched (AIG-cloned) relations reduces the conditional standard error near the cut, so borderline children get more matched items before a decision, while M-DIFFREACH tracks the hardest relation family solved.
age_rationale: Explicit relational mapping over symbols suits grade 2 and up with simple additive relations and candidate answers; 4-5 introduces multiplicative relations and 3x3 matrices; 6-8 adds two-rule matrices and fraction/ratio relations. Tap/keypad answer is low motor. K-1 is excluded because symbolic relational mapping exceeds typical readiness.

adaptive.content_range: single additive 2x2 analogies (2-3) through multiplicative and two-rule 3x3 numeric matrices with fraction/ratio relations (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: relation type (additive/multiplicative/mixed), 2x2 vs 3x3, one vs two simultaneous relations, number magnitude/format, candidate vs free entry, and distractor design (additive foil present).
adaptive.notes: Relations sampled parametrically; matched clones support M-CONSIST; foils computed from common misreads.

engagement_hook: A glowing relation-arrow the child can replay to watch the transformation animate; solving feels like decoding a secret link between numbers rather than filling in a worksheet analogy.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Keypad entry adds motor and numeral load (offer candidate-tap for young bands); ensure distractors do not leak the answer by elimination; no reading required; keep magnitudes small so the bottleneck is the relation, not computation.

name: Ratio Mixer
topics_techniques_covered: proportional_reasoning: ratio/rate unit reasoning (e.g., exchange rate, best-buy comparison)
quantitative_comparison of ratios
word_problem_reasoning: rate reasoning
equivalent fractions and ratios
one_liner: The child adjusts quantities (scoops of two ingredients, or price vs amount) to match a target ratio or to pick the equivalent or better-value option.
interaction: Two connected quantities are shown as adjustable scoops/bars/sliders (e.g., a 2 red : 3 blue mixture, or a price for N items). The child either (a) adjusts one quantity so a second mixture matches the target ratio, with a 'taste-match' color meter showing closeness (not the numeric answer), or (b) taps which of two options is the better buy or equivalent ratio. Submission = Serve/confirm. Strategy (scaling both quantities vs adding a constant) is inferred from the move sequence.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a target glass is 1 red : 1 blue (purple); a second glass has 2 red, so the hand adds blue scoops one at a time until the color-match meter turns full green at 2 blue, then serves. Unscored warm-up: match 1:1 given one red already placed. The color meter teaches 'same ratio = same color' without numbers or words.

learning_science.principle: Proportional reasoning develops from additive to multiplicative
learning_science.why: Learners often misuse additive strategies on proportion problems; distinguishing multiplicative (ratio-preserving) from additive responders is a hallmark of higher quantitative reasoning and predicts later math.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use non-integer, non-doubling targets where an additive strategy gives a specific wrong mixture, and log whether adjustments preserve the ratio (multiplicative) or a difference (additive).
learning_science.source: Noelting (1980), 'The development of proportional reasoning and the ratio concept: Part I - Differentiation of stages', Educational Studies in Mathematics 11(2):217-253.

learning_science.principle: Perceptual grounding of ratio (mixture/part-whole)
learning_science.why: Representing ratio as a perceptible quantity (color intensity, fullness) lets children reason proportionally before mastering fraction notation, broadening who can demonstrate the reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Render the ratio as a continuous perceptual cue (mixture color/needle) that reflects closeness to the target ratio without revealing the numeric answer.
learning_science.source: Boyer, Levine & Huttenlocher (2008), 'Development of proportional reasoning: Where young children go wrong', Developmental Psychology 44(5):1478-1490.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Proportional strategy signature (multiplicative vs additive)
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Classifies whether the child preserves the ratio (multiplicative/scaling) or a constant difference (additive) during adjustments, the decisive divide in proportional reasoning that a correct/incorrect score cannot see; isolates genuine proportional reasoners at the tail.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: From the move sequence, fit whether successive adjustments hold the quantity-ratio constant vs the quantity-difference constant, classify the strategy, and record consistency across items.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=4-6 proportion items including non-integer/non-doubling targets to classify strategy reliably.

tail_precision_rationale: M-PROPSTRAT plus efficiency-vs-optimal separate multiplicative reasoners from additive approximators even when both eventually land correct, and non-integer targets prevent doubling shortcuts, concentrating discrimination on the reasoning that defines the upper tail of quantitative ability.
age_rationale: Robust proportional reasoning is later-developing; simple doubling can appear by grade 4, so 4-5 uses integer/doubling ratios while 6-8 uses non-integer ratios, rates, and best-buy comparisons. Slider/scoop adjustment is well within motor range. K-1 and 2-3 are excluded because proportional reasoning is typically pre-emergent there, keeping coverage honest.

adaptive.content_range: integer/doubling mixtures (4-5) through non-integer ratios, unit-rate, and best-buy reasoning (6-8); the mixer shell reaches ratio/rate reasoning that normally needs fraction notation.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: integer vs non-integer target ratio, doubling vs non-doubling, number of parts, discrete scoops vs continuous slider, match-the-ratio vs pick-better-value, presence of an additive-trap distractor, and rate (per-unit) framing.
adaptive.notes: Targets generated as ratios; additive-trap answers computed; the perceptual meter is derived from ratio distance for M-PROG.

engagement_hook: A mixing/potion game where getting the ratio right turns the color exactly to the target and serves it; proportional reasoning becomes tuning a color rather than manipulating fractions.
construct_irrelevant_risks: The color meter could allow pure color-matching without numeric reasoning (include no-meter commit-blind scored items and log strategy); slider precision (snap to sensible increments, scale tolerance); avoid reading with iconic ingredients; provide non-color backups for color-vision differences.

name: Story Model Builder
topics_techniques_covered: word_problem_reasoning: multi-step and nonroutine problems
model two growing quantities and find where they are equal (PISA Apples)
bar-model representation of a word problem
multi-constraint reasoning; short constructed numeric response
one_liner: The child builds a visual model (adjustable bars, two growing stacks, or tokens) of a short illustrated story problem and manipulates it to find the answer.
interaction: A short story is presented with icons and minimal or audio text (e.g., two plants growing at different rates). The child manipulates a model: drag to set bar lengths, step two quantities forward turn-by-turn, or place tokens to satisfy constraints, with a live readout of current values. For find-where-equal the child advances until the two quantities meet and marks that point; for bar-model problems the child sizes bars then reads or enters the answer. Submission = Answer with the modeled value; partial credit is captured from model correctness even if the final number is off.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): two seedlings; plant A starts at 2 and grows +1/day, plant B starts at 0 and grows +2/day; the hand taps 'next day' stepping both, the bars rise, and when they meet at day 2 (both = 4) a flag pops on the equal point. Unscored warm-up: step until a 1+1 stack equals a 2 stack. Watching the bars grow and meet teaches the find-where-equal goal wordlessly.

learning_science.principle: Model method / bar modeling
learning_science.why: Representing word-problem structure with proportional bars scaffolds reasoning about unknowns and relations without symbols and is a validated route to solving multi-step problems.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide draggable proportional bars as the response medium so the child expresses the problem structure, and score the model's structural correctness separately from the final number.
learning_science.source: Ng & Lee (2009), 'The model method: Singapore children's tool for representing and solving algebraic word problems', Journal for Research in Mathematics Education 40(3):282-313.

learning_science.principle: Covariational reasoning (two changing quantities)
learning_science.why: Reasoning about how two quantities co-vary and when they coincide is core quantitative reasoning (the PISA Apples task) and predicts later functions and algebra understanding.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include a 'two growing quantities, find where equal' interactive where the child steps time and observes the meeting point, capturing covariation reasoning directly.
learning_science.source: Carlson, Jacobs, Coe, Larsen & Hsu (2002), 'Applying covariational reasoning while modeling dynamic events: A framework and a study', Journal for Research in Mathematics Education 33(5):352-378.

tail_precision_rationale: Partial-credit scoring of the model (structure right, arithmetic slip) extracts tail information from one rich item like several dichotomous items and rescues near-miss latent ability; progress trajectory and persistence on hard multi-step items add a task-commitment signal (Renzulli) that pure accuracy misses, sharpening decisions among high performers who differ in how they push through difficulty.
age_rationale: Multi-step modeling and covariation reasoning require sustained working memory and inference typical from grade 4 up; 4-5 uses single-model, small-number problems while 6-8 uses multi-step, multi-constraint, and non-integer covariation. Audio narration removes decoding load. K-1 and 2-3 are excluded because multi-step model construction exceeds typical readiness, keeping coverage honest.

adaptive.content_range: single bar-model or small covariation problems (4-5) through multi-step, multi-constraint, and non-integer rate covariation (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of steps/constraints, integer vs non-integer rates, single vs multiple bars, magnitude, pre-structured vs built-from-scratch model, and audio vs text framing.
adaptive.notes: Story templates with swappable quantities/rates; partial-credit rubric tied to model structure; lower AIG cloneability than pure-numeric shells because narrative framing needs curation to avoid reading confounds.

engagement_hook: A story comes alive as a growing diagram the child controls; stepping time to watch two plants race and 'catch' the moment they are equal turns a word problem into an interactive animation.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Reading/language load is the biggest risk (mitigate with icons, audio narration, and minimal text); working-memory load on multi-step items (keep live readouts visible); motor drag for bars (snap increments); the wordless demo must make the model buildable without prior bar-model schooling; the partial-credit rubric must not reward random dragging.

name: Story Stage (Act-It-Out)
topics_techniques_covered: word_problem_reasoning
act-it-out / direct modeling of join, separate, part-part-whole, equal-share and compare structures
multi-step open-response math problem (grade 4)
nonroutine logic or number puzzle (grades 3-4)
short constructed response: solve and explain a numeric result
arithmetic_reasoning
one_liner: The child acts out a short illustrated story by moving concrete objects into groups, plates, or containers until the situation is modeled, and the final arrangement is the answer.
interaction: An illustrated one- or multi-step story is shown with icons and optional audio (no required reading). The child enacts it directly on a stage: tap a plate/box/group to move one object into it from the tray, tap a placed object to send it back, combining, separating, sharing, or comparing groups until the story is satisfied (for example share all treats so every plate is equal). A live per-group count updates. Submission = Done; scoring reads the final arrangement, and partial credit is awarded for a structurally correct model even if a count is off.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): six treats are dealt one at a time, alternating between two plates, until both plates hold three and a chime plays; the hand repeats the round-robin once. One unscored warm-up shares four treats between two plates with a wide equal cue. Watching objects physically move into equal groups teaches share/group/compare with zero words.

learning_science.principle: Direct modeling / act-it-out problem solving (Cognitively Guided Instruction)
learning_science.why: Young children reliably solve arithmetic word problems by directly modeling the actions and quantities with objects long before they master symbolic strategies, so enactment lets word-problem reasoning be demonstrated without notation or reading.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide concrete movable objects and containers as the answer medium so the child enacts join/separate/equal-share/compare, and score the modeled structure with partial credit separately from any final count.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, Fennema, Franke, Levi & Empson (1999), 'Children's Mathematics: Cognitively Guided Instruction', Heinemann.

learning_science.principle: Semantic problem structures (change/combine/compare/equalize)
learning_science.why: Word-problem difficulty is driven by the semantic structure and the position of the unknown rather than the surface numbers, so matching the manipulative to the structure exposes which structures a child can reason about.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Generate items across change, combine, compare, and equal-share structures with different unknown positions, and tag each error by the structure and the operation the child enacted.
learning_science.source: Riley, Greeno & Heller (1983), 'Development of children's problem-solving ability in arithmetic', in Ginsburg (ed.), The Development of Mathematical Thinking, Academic Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Partial-credit scoring of the enacted model extracts several bits from one rich item and rescues near-miss latent ability (right structure, miscount), while the move path and efficiency-vs-optimal separate children who deal systematically (round-robin sharing, one-to-one matching) from brute or random moving; persistence/time-on-task on hard multi-step stories adds a task-commitment signal that pure accuracy misses at the tail.
age_rationale: Concrete direct modeling is the youngest-accessible route to word problems: K-1 enacts single-step join/separate/equal-share with small numbers and large tap targets; 2-3 and 4-5 add larger quantities and two-step stories; 6-8 add multi-step and multi-constraint enactment. The tap-to-move interaction is constant and reading is removed via icons/audio, deliberately broadening who can demonstrate word-problem reasoning.

adaptive.content_range: one-step join/separate/equal-share with small numbers (K-1) through multi-step, multi-group sharing and comparison stories (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of steps, structure type (change/combine/compare/equalize), quantity magnitude, number of groups/containers, unknown position (result vs start vs change), and integer vs remainder shares.
adaptive.notes: Story shells parameterize quantities and structure; the optimal move count is known for M-EFF and the target arrangement for M-POLY; narrative framing needs light curation to avoid reading confounds, lowering cloneability below pure-numeric shells.

engagement_hook: A hands-on stage where treats physically slide onto plates and a chime rewards a perfectly fair share, so a word problem becomes a tactile dealing game rather than a text to decode.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Fine-motor/tap load (large targets, tap-to-move instead of precise drag, undo by tapping a placed object); reading/language (icons + optional audio, no required text); brute-force dealing instead of reasoning (captured via M-EFF/M-PATH rather than penalized outright); ensure the wordless demo makes the goal obvious without prior schooling; the partial-credit rubric must not reward random object moving.

name: Deduction Grid
topics_techniques_covered: word_problem_reasoning
nonroutine logic or number puzzle (grades 3-4)
multi-constraint reasoning sample (grades 5-6)
number_properties_reasoning
reason about number properties (even/odd, factors) or how to create the largest result
deductive constraint satisfaction (logic-grid elimination)
one_liner: The child cross-references picture-and-symbol clues to deduce which quantity belongs to each character, marking a possibility grid with no (cross) and yes (check).
interaction: A small grid pairs characters (rows) with candidate numbers (columns). A few clues appear as icon chips using only comparison symbols (for example cat < rabbit, dog > rabbit) or property icons (even, factor). The child taps a cell to cycle blank -> cross (impossible) -> check (must be true), eliminating options until each character has exactly one number. Submission = Check; the grid is graded against the unique consistent solution. No arithmetic entry or reading is required.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): on a two-by-two grid with the clue cat < dog, the hand crosses out the cells a clue forbids, then checks the two forced cells, and a chime confirms cat=1, dog=2. One unscored single-clue two-by-two warm-up teaches the blank -> cross -> check tap and the idea of eliminating impossibilities wordlessly.

learning_science.principle: Deductive reasoning by elimination / mental models
learning_science.why: Nonroutine logic puzzles require holding several constraints and eliminating impossible combinations to reach a forced conclusion, a form of deductive reasoning distinct from computation and central to quantitative problem solving.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Render the possibility space as an explicit grid and let the child externalize eliminations, so the reasoning process (not just the final assignment) is observable and scorable.
learning_science.source: Johnson-Laird (1983), 'Mental Models: Towards a Cognitive Science of Language, Inference, and Consciousness', Harvard University Press.

learning_science.principle: Relational complexity limits simultaneous constraint integration
learning_science.why: The number of constraints that must be considered jointly sets item difficulty; children who integrate more interacting relations at once are demonstrating higher-order reasoning that a single computation cannot reveal.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scale the number of interacting clues and entities and design clues so each additional constraint must be combined with others, then record the hardest constraint count a child solves.
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), 'Processing capacity defined by relational complexity', Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6):803-831.

tail_precision_rationale: Hypothesis-search efficiency (the share of the child's marks that are logically valid eliminations, and how quickly the possibility space collapses) indexes deductive/scientific reasoning and dynamic-assessment learning rate beyond final accuracy, resisting coaching; M-DIFFREACH over increasing clue counts pinpoints the relational-complexity ceiling that most sharply separates the upper tail.
age_rationale: Cross-referencing multiple constraints is beyond typical K-1 readiness, so K-1 is excluded to stay honest. 2-3 uses a minimal two-by-two with one clue taught by the demo; 4-5 uses three-by-three grids with two to three ordered clues; 6-8 adds four entities, property clues (even/odd, factor), and chains requiring several combined inferences. The blank/cross/check tap is constant and low motor.

adaptive.content_range: single-clue two-by-two deduction (2-3) through four-entity grids with combined ordering and number-property clues (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size, number of clues, clue type (ordering, equality, parity/factor), how many inferences must be chained, and whether any clue is redundant or every clue is load-bearing.
adaptive.notes: Puzzles are generated by sampling a solution then emitting a minimal load-bearing clue set with a checked unique-solution guarantee; M-HYP compares each mark to the entailed eliminations.

engagement_hook: A detective crack-the-case feel: each cross rules a suspect out and the final checks snap the answer into place, turning multi-constraint word problems into a satisfying deduction puzzle.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Reading load (clues are icon + comparison-symbol chips, not sentences); working-memory load of tracking constraints (the grid externalizes state so it is not a memory test); guess-and-check filling (captured via M-HYP and the valid-mark ratio rather than a raw solve flag); ensure symbols are distinguishable without color alone.

name: Solution Recipe (Step Planner)
topics_techniques_covered: word_problem_reasoning
multi-step open-response math problem (grade 4)
multi-step quantitative reasoning problem (grades 6-8)
number_sentence_building
enter values to make a relation true or balance both sides of an equation
arithmetic_reasoning
one_liner: The child solves a multi-step story by assembling an ordered chain of operation steps, each showing its intermediate result, which can feed the next step.
interaction: A short illustrated story is shown with icons and optional audio. Below it are empty step rows, each a slot template number-operator-number that auto-computes an equals result when filled. The child taps a slot to select it, then taps number or operator chips from a palette; a completed step's result becomes a new chip that can be used in later steps. The last step's result is the answer. Submission = Answer; each step is scored so partial credit is earned for correct sub-steps even if a later step slips.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): for a share-then-take story, the hand fills step one as 12 divided by 3 equals 4, the 4 pops out as a new chip, then fills step two as 4 times 2 equals 8, and a chime confirms the answer. One unscored one-step warm-up (5 + 3) teaches the tap-a-slot then tap-a-chip mechanic wordlessly.

learning_science.principle: Problem decomposition and means-ends planning
learning_science.why: Multi-step problems are solved by decomposing the goal into ordered sub-goals and chaining operations, and the quality of that plan separates strong quantitative reasoners from those who can compute but cannot structure a solution.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Make the sub-goal structure the response medium (an explicit ordered chain of operation steps with visible intermediate results) and award partial credit per correct sub-goal.
learning_science.source: Newell & Simon (1972), 'Human Problem Solving', Prentice-Hall.

learning_science.principle: Sub-goal learning and labeling
learning_science.why: Making the sub-goal structure of a multi-step procedure explicit supports transfer and reveals whether a child grasps the structural steps rather than only the surface arithmetic.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Externalize each sub-goal as a labeled step tile so structural planning is scored separately from computation, and tag errors as wrong-operation versus wrong-number versus wrong-order.
learning_science.source: Catrambone (1998), 'The subgoal learning model: Creating better examples so that students can solve novel problems', Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 127(4):355-376.

tail_precision_rationale: Per-step partial credit turns one multi-step item into several ordered dichotomies, extracting tail information and rescuing structure-right/arithmetic-wrong near-misses; the progress trajectory across steps and error-type tagging (wrong-operation vs wrong-number vs wrong-order) distinguish planful decomposers from children who guess a single operation, sharpening decisions among high performers who all reach a final number.
age_rationale: Decomposing a problem into an ordered multi-step plan requires sustained working memory and planning typical from grade 4 up, so K-1 and 2-3 are excluded to keep coverage honest. 4-5 uses two-step problems with small numbers; 6-8 uses three-step and multi-constraint problems with larger numbers and mixed operations. Audio narration removes decoding load and the tap-slot/tap-chip entry is low motor.

adaptive.content_range: two-step arithmetic stories (4-5) through three-step, mixed-operation, multi-constraint problems (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of steps, operation set, whether an intermediate result must be reused, magnitude, presence of a distractor number, and predetermined vs free step count.
adaptive.notes: Story templates swap quantities and operations with a stored correct step chain for M-POLY and known optimal edit count for M-EFF; narrative curation to avoid reading confounds lowers cloneability below pure-numeric shells.

engagement_hook: Building a recipe of steps where each result pops out as a new ingredient chip to drop into the next step makes multi-step reasoning feel like assembling a machine rather than writing out a computation.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Reading load (icons + audio, minimal text); arithmetic-fact load could mask reasoning (cap number sizes and let the machine compute each step so planning, not calculation, is the bottleneck); guessing a single operation (mitigated by per-step scoring and error typing); ensure operator chips are legible and the active slot is clearly indicated.

name: Growing Pattern Architect
topics_techniques_covered: pattern_completion
generalize a growing figural-number pattern to the nth case and justify the relationship
reason across figural and numeric representations of a pattern (step pattern / number cubes)
extend a repeating or growing pattern and state the rule
number_series
continue an early pictorial pattern or quantity sequence
one_liner: The child studies the first few stages of a growing tile figure and builds (or, for far stages, dials) the next stage so the figural-and-numeric pattern keeps going.
interaction: Stages 1 to 3 of a growing pattern are shown as small tile figures with their counts. For near stages the child builds the next figure by tapping cells on a grid while a live tile count updates; for a far stage (for example stage 10) the child instead dials the count with plus/minus steppers. Submission = Done; the built count (or dialed value) is graded against the stage's true size. Clear resets the build.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): stages of 1, 2, 3 tiles are shown growing by one, and the hand builds stage four by tapping four cells one at a time as the counter climbs, then a chime confirms. One unscored warm-up asks the child to build the next stage of a plus-two pattern. Watching the figure grow by a fixed amount teaches extend-the-pattern with no words.

learning_science.principle: Pattern generalization as a route into algebra
learning_science.why: Extending growing figural patterns and generalizing to the nth case is a validated pathway into algebraic generalization, and children can express generality figurally before they have symbols, lowering the notation barrier to higher-order reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Ask for both a near stage (build the next figure) and a far stage (dial the nth count) so near-versus-far transfer distinguishes children who project an explicit functional rule from those limited to recursive counting.
learning_science.source: Lannin (2005), 'Generalization and justification: The challenge of introducing algebraic reasoning through pattern exploration', Mathematical Thinking and Learning 7(3):231-258.

learning_science.principle: Connecting figural and numeric representations of a pattern
learning_science.why: Coordinating the figure with its count deepens structural (functional) understanding over merely recursive extension, and the actions a child uses to build a far term reveal whether they see the underlying structure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Show each stage as both a figure and a number and let the child construct stages, so recursive (+step) versus explicit (functional) strategies are visible in how the far term is built.
learning_science.source: Warren & Cooper (2008), 'Generalising the pattern rule for visual growth patterns', Educational Studies in Mathematics 67(2):171-185.

tail_precision_rationale: Requiring construction (not selection) exposes strategy: efficiency-vs-optimal and the build path separate children who place exactly the structural number of tiles from those who add and remove by trial; M-RULEID captures how many co-acting growth features (constant, linear, or second-order) the child integrates, and near-versus-far M-DIFFREACH (stage four vs stage ten) isolates explicit functional generalization, the reasoning that defines the quantitative tail.
age_rationale: Building the next stage of a pattern is accessible across the range: K-1 extends simple repeating or plus-one growth by placing tiles; 2-3 and 4-5 handle linear growth and near-stage generalization; 6-8 handle second-order (triangular) growth and far/nth-stage generalization via the dial. The tap-to-build and dial interactions are constant and require no notation.

adaptive.content_range: repeating and plus-one growth (K-1) through second-order growth and nth-term generalization (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: growth rule (constant, linear, second-order), near vs far stage requested, build vs dial response, number magnitude, and whether the figure encodes one or two co-acting features.
adaptive.notes: Stages are generated from parametric growth families with a known count per stage for M-ACC/M-EFF and a rule-dimensionality tag for M-RULEID; distractor sizes follow common recursive-vs-functional confusions.

engagement_hook: Being the architect who builds the next piece of a growing structure (and predicting a far-off stage) turns pattern generalization into a construction game where the shape visibly grows under the child's taps.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Fine-motor tap load for larger builds (offer the dial for far/large stages so building many tiles is never required); brute add/remove instead of structural reasoning (captured via M-EFF/M-PATH); no reading required (figures + counts); ensure the example stages stay visible throughout so it is not a memory test.

name: Equation Forge
topics_techniques_covered: number_sentence_building
enter values to make a relation true or balance both sides of an equation
mathematical-equivalence items (meaning of the equal sign, e.g. 3+4=_+5)
Number Puzzles: choose the value that balances both sides / solves for the missing part
number_properties_reasoning
reason about number properties (even/odd, factors) or how to create the largest result
arithmetic_reasoning
one_liner: The child drops a number tile into a blank on a symbolic number sentence so that both sides are equal, with the equals sign lighting up when the sentence becomes true.
interaction: A number sentence with a blank is shown, often non-canonical (for example 3 + 4 = _ + 5). Live side totals are displayed and the equals sign turns green the instant both sides match. The child taps a number tile from a palette to fill the blank and may retap other tiles to change it; a target-number variant asks the child to combine given tiles to reach a goal or make the largest result. Submission = Check. The first tile placed is recorded to reveal strategy before any adjustment.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): for 2 + 3 = _ + 1 the hand reaches for the 4 tile, drops it in the blank, both side totals read 5, and the equals sign glows green with a chime. One unscored warm-up (4 = _ + 1) teaches tap-a-tile-into-the-box and the both-sides-equal goal via the live totals, with no words.

learning_science.principle: Relational understanding of the equal sign
learning_science.why: Many children hold an operational view of the equal sign (the answer comes next); a relational view (both sides name the same amount) uniquely predicts later algebra success, and building a true non-canonical sentence requires that relational view.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use non-canonical sentences with a blank on the right and include the operational-error tile (the running total of the visible left side) as a distractor, then classify the child's first placement as relational or operational.
learning_science.source: McNeil & Alibali (2005), 'Why won't you change your mind? Knowledge of operational patterns hinders learning and performance on equations', Child Development 76(4):883-899.

learning_science.principle: Flexible mental calculation / combinatorial number sense
learning_science.why: Composing given numbers and operations to hit a target (as in make-a-number games) exercises strategic, flexible arithmetic and number-property reasoning rather than rote calculation, which marks stronger quantitative reasoners.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer a target-number/largest-result variant with a small set of number and operator tiles and score the strategy and efficiency of the search, not just the final value.
learning_science.source: Threlfall (2002), 'Flexible mental calculation', Educational Studies in Mathematics 50(1):29-47.

tail_precision_rationale: The equivalence signature (M-EQREL) from the first tile placed flags relational versus operational thinking, a research-backed early separator of algebra-ready reasoning that dichotomous accuracy hides; exploration count and efficiency-vs-optimal (moves versus the single correct placement) distinguish children who compute the needed value directly from those who try tiles until the sign turns green, concentrating information exactly where pre-algebraic talent emerges.
age_rationale: Manipulating a symbolic number sentence to make it true suits grade 2 and up; K-1 is excluded because reasoning over operator/number symbols exceeds typical readiness. 2-3 uses small whole-number canonical and simple non-canonical sentences; 4-5 uses non-canonical equivalence and missing-addend puzzles; 6-8 adds multi-term sentences, target/largest-result search, and fraction or property constraints. The tap-a-tile interaction is constant and low motor.

adaptive.content_range: small whole-number sentences (2-3) through non-canonical multi-term equivalence and target/largest-result puzzles with property constraints (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: canonical vs non-canonical form, blank position, number of terms/blanks, presence of the operational-trap tile, magnitude and format (whole/fraction), and make-true vs make-target vs make-largest goal.
adaptive.notes: Sentences are generated from equivalence and target templates with the operational-trap distractor computed automatically; the single-placement optimum drives M-EFF and the first-pick classification drives M-EQREL.

engagement_hook: A satisfying forge where the equals sign snaps green and chimes the instant both sides balance, turning equation building and the meaning of the equal sign into a quick puzzle of getting two totals to match.
construct_irrelevant_risks: The live side totals could allow trial-and-error balancing without reasoning (the first-placement M-EQREL classification and efficiency capture strategy, and commit-blind target variants in the item bank remove the meter); minimal reading (symbols and numerals only); ensure tiles are legible and the equals-sign state is shown by more than color alone.

name: Skip-Count Orbit
topics_techniques_covered: number_series
Number Series: find the beads/number that continue an ordered numeric series
Number Series: determine the missing number in a sequence (Gf/RQ)
continue an early pictorial pattern or quantity sequence
number_sense_magnitude
skip-counting and cyclic/modular sequence continuation on a circular scale
one_liner: A token hops around a numbered ring by a constant jump; the child taps the cell where it lands next, extending an ordered (and sometimes wrapping) numeric series.
interaction: Numbered cells are arranged in a circle with a hub showing the constant jump. The first few landings of a skip-count are highlighted and connected by arcs, with the next landing left blank. The child taps the ring cell where the token lands next; on harder items the jump carries the count past the top of the ring so it must wrap around (modular). Response = a single tap, auto-committed. Matched clone items (same jump, different start) probe consistency.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the token starts at 0 and the hand hops it +2 around the ring to 2, 4, 6 with a glowing arc each jump, then taps 8 and a chime plays. One unscored warm-up hops +1 so the tap-where-it-lands-next rule is obvious; the arcs make the constant jump visible with no words.

learning_science.principle: Skip counting and the structure of the number sequence
learning_science.why: Skip counting builds multiplicative structure and fluent number-sequence knowledge that underpins later arithmetic, and predicting landing positions on a track indexes how well a child projects an ordered numeric series.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Present the series as landings of a constant jump around a track and score the child's projection of the next landing, scaling the jump size to probe skip-count fluency.
learning_science.source: Fuson (1988), 'Children's Counting and Concepts of Number', Springer-Verlag.

learning_science.principle: Inductive rule projection on cyclic/modular structure
learning_science.why: Continuing a sequence requires inducing the generating rule and projecting it; wrapping the count around a ring adds a modular constraint so that naive linear continuation fails, separating children who track the cyclic structure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include modular-wrap items where the next landing exceeds the ring size, and tag near-misses as no-wrap (linear guess) versus off-by-one to reveal the failure mode.
learning_science.source: Holzman, Pellegrino & Glaser (1983), 'Cognitive variables in series completion', Journal of Educational Psychology 75(4):603-618.

tail_precision_rationale: First-action latency indexes planning (reflective solvers compute the landing before tapping) while M-DIFFREACH over increasing jump sizes and modular wraps pinpoints the hardest series a child projects; matched-clone consistency (M-CONSIST) reduces the conditional standard error near the cut so borderline children are decided on parallel items rather than a single lucky tap.
age_rationale: Continuing a count on a track spans the range: K-1 hops by ones and twos on a small ring (a counting/skip-counting task); 2-3 and 4-5 use larger jumps and full skip-count series; 6-8 add modular wraps and larger rings that require projecting the rule past the top of the ring. The single-tap response is the lowest motor demand and no reading is needed.

adaptive.content_range: count-by-one and count-by-two on a small ring (K-1) through larger jumps and modular-wrap continuation on bigger rings (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: jump size, ring size (modulus), whether the next landing wraps, number of landings shown before the blank, and start offset for matched clones.
adaptive.notes: Items are fully generated from (ring size, start, step, count shown); matched clones share step/modulus with a different start for M-CONSIST, and the wrap flag sets the M-DIFFREACH difficulty.

engagement_hook: A token orbiting a ring and snapping onto its next landing spot makes skip counting and number-series continuation feel like an orbital arcade game, with wraps around the ring as a fun twist.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Rewarding raw speed (first-action latency is logged for planning, not scored as fastest-wins, and accuracy gates the signal); motor precision (large ring cells, single tap); no reading required (numerals and arcs); ensure visited and target states are distinguishable without relying on color alone.

name: Bead Rack Reasoner
topics_techniques_covered: number_series
Number Series: find the beads/number that continue an ordered numeric series
quantitative_comparison: compare two magnitudes and judge greater / less / equal
number_sense_magnitude
approximate number system dot-comparison: choose the array with more dots
quantitative_reasoning_mixed: verbal and nonverbal number problems and patterns
one_liner: The child slides beads on a two-row rack to continue a number series, show a target quantity, or compare two racks and say which shows more.
interaction: A rekenrek-style rack shows one or two rows of ten beads grouped in fives. A spoken-and-pictured prompt sets the task: (a) continue a series - the rack shows the beads for the first terms and the child slides beads on the next rack to the term that comes next; (b) show a magnitude - slide exactly the target number of beads; or (c) compare - two racks are shown and the child taps the rack with more, or a center EQUAL button. Beads move by tapping a bead (all beads up to it slide to the active side) or dragging the group, and a live count shows above each row. Submission = Lock (series/build) or a single tap (compare), with a short redrag window before commit.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the rack shows 2 then 4 then 6 beads on successive rows with a glowing +2 arc, and a translucent hand slides 8 beads onto the last rack and locks with a chime; a compare round then flashes two racks and the hand taps the fuller one. One unscored warm-up asks the child to slide beads to continue 1, 2, 3 with a wide success band. The five-structure and sliding action make show-this-many and which-is-more obvious without words.

learning_science.principle: Subitizing and the five/ten structure of quantity
learning_science.why: Grouping beads in fives lets children perceive and compose quantities without one-by-one counting, exposing magnitude and number-structure understanding before symbolic fluency and broadening who can show quantitative talent.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a five-structured rack so responses reveal five-and-ten composition (for example 8 as 5+3), and score the composition strategy alongside the final count.
learning_science.source: Clements (1999), 'Subitizing: What is it? Why teach it?', Teaching Children Mathematics 5(7):400-405.

learning_science.principle: Analogue magnitude distance effect
learning_science.why: Comparison speed and accuracy scale with the numerical distance between two quantities, so an adaptive comparison ratio yields a fine-grained, low-literacy index of magnitude precision that keeps separating children after symbolic items ceiling.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include flashed compare rounds with an adaptive distance/ratio between the two racks and credit accuracy-held speed rather than raw speed.
learning_science.source: Moyer & Landauer (1967), 'Time required for judgements of numerical inequality', Nature 215:1519-1520.

tail_precision_rationale: Adaptive escalation of series step and compare distance yields M-DIFFREACH (the hardest series and closest comparison a child resolves), the sharpest single tail statistic; a stable speed-accuracy operating point credits fluency only when accuracy holds, and matched-clone consistency (M-CONSIST) shrinks the conditional standard error near the cut so borderline children are decided on parallel racks rather than one lucky slide.
age_rationale: Sliding beads and tapping the fuller rack are among the lowest motor demands, so the shell runs from K-1 (continue 1,2,3; show small quantities; compare obvious rows) upward, with series step size, compare ratio, and two-row two-digit magnitudes escalating for older bands. The K-8 tag marks that the same concrete rack spans the whole range via adaptive difficulty rather than a change of interaction, and reading is removed by spoken plus pictured prompts.

adaptive.content_range: count/compare/continue within 10 (K-1) through two-row two-digit magnitude, larger skip-count series, and fine-ratio comparison (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: series step and rule, compare ratio/distance, one vs two rows (ten vs twenty/two-digit), flashed-then-masked vs static compare, and build-exact vs continue-series task
adaptive.notes: Series, targets and compare pairs are generated numerically; matched clones (same step, different start) drive M-CONSIST and the compare-ratio staircase drives M-DIFFREACH.

engagement_hook: Beads snap across the rack in satisfying groups of five and a compare round plays like a quick which-pile-is-bigger reflex game, so counting structure and magnitude feel like sliding an abacus rather than doing sums.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor precision when sliding many beads (tap-to-fill and snap-to-count reduce it); rewarding raw speed on compares (credit only accuracy-held speed via M-SPEEDACC, never the fastest tap); density/size confounds in nonsymbolic compares (control bead spacing and include size-number-incongruent rows); reading removed via spoken and pictured prompts; keep EQUAL reachable to avoid position bias.

name: Hanging Mobile Balancer
topics_techniques_covered: balance_equivalence: choose the weight(s) that keep a balance scale in equilibrium (Figure Weights)
number_sentence_building: enter values to balance both sides of an equation
mathematical-equivalence items (meaning of the equal sign, e.g. 3+4=_+5)
arithmetic_reasoning
proportional_reasoning: ratio/rate reasoning via lever distance (torque)
one_liner: The child hangs shapes on the hooks of a tilting mobile so every arm hangs perfectly level, discovering the weight or position that makes both sides equal.
interaction: A mobile hangs from a pivot: a horizontal bar with hooks at marked distances on each side (older levels add a second sub-bar). Each shape carries a hidden weight shown as pips. The child drags shapes onto hooks (or into an empty target hook) and the bar tilts in real time toward the heavier turning-effect side; when both sides match, the bar snaps level and glows. Tasks: make it hang level, or choose which single weight fills the empty hook to balance. Submission = Lock when level. A missing-addend / non-canonical variant pre-loads unequal sides so only a relational solution levels it, and for older bands hook distance matters so a light shape far out can balance a heavy shape near in.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the left hook holds 3 pips and the right holds 1 so the bar tips left; the hand drags a 2-pip shape onto the right and the bar swings level with a settle and chime, then repeats once. One unscored warm-up hangs one apple opposite one apple to level a simple bar. The tilt makes level-means-equal obvious with no words.

learning_science.principle: Rule-based development of balance-scale reasoning (weight then distance)
learning_science.why: Children progress through identifiable rules on balance tasks - weight-only, then integrating distance - so a mobile is a validated probe that scales from concrete equality to multiplicative torque reasoning within one shell.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer weight-only leveling for young bands and distance-matters (torque) items for older bands, and infer the child's rule level from which items they can balance.
learning_science.source: Siegler & Chen (1998), 'Developmental differences in rule learning: A microgenetic analysis', Cognitive Psychology 36(3):273-310.

learning_science.principle: Relational meaning of the equal sign
learning_science.why: A relational view of equality (both sides name the same amount) rather than an operational one uniquely predicts later algebra success, and leveling a pre-loaded unequal mobile requires that relational view.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use non-canonical pre-loaded sides and classify the child's first hang as relational (targets the needed remainder) or operational (dumps a running total).
learning_science.source: Kieran (1981), 'Concepts associated with the equality symbol', Educational Studies in Mathematics 12(3):317-326.

tail_precision_rationale: The equivalence signature (M-EQREL) from the first hang flags relational versus operational thinking - a research-backed early separator of algebra-ready reasoning invisible to a right/wrong score - while on distance items the proportional-strategy signature (M-PROPSTRAT) distinguishes children who trade weight against distance multiplicatively from those who only add weight; efficiency-vs-optimal and revisions separate direct computers from tilt-guided trial and error.
