age_rationale: As a concrete make-it-hang-straight matching task the mobile is accessible at K-1 (equal counts on symmetric hooks); genuine equivalence reasoning (missing-addend, non-canonical sides) emerges at 2-3 and up, and distance/torque proportional balancing is reserved for 6-8. The drag-to-hook interaction is constant, and the K-8 tag reflects one shell spanning concrete equality through pre-algebraic torque via adaptive difficulty.

adaptive.content_range: concrete symmetric leveling with equal counts (K-1) through non-canonical missing-addend equivalence (2-3/4-5) and multiplicative distance/torque balancing that encodes proportional relationships without notation (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of hooks and shapes, canonical vs non-canonical pre-load, weight-only vs distance-matters, integer vs fractional weights, and number of empty target hooks
adaptive.notes: Hook loads and distances are generated from equivalence and torque templates; the operational-trap load is computed for M-EQREL and the optimal hang count for M-EFF.

engagement_hook: A dangling mobile that sways and teeters like a real hanging sculpture and snaps satisfyingly level when balanced turns equivalence and lever reasoning into a mobile-building game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Drag motor load (snap-to-hook, large shapes); pure tilt-guided trial and error (captured via M-EFF and the first-hang M-EQREL rather than penalized, with some commit-blind items in the bank); reading removed via pips and icons; tilt state shown by angle and a level-line, not color alone; distance items use clearly marked hook positions so the lever arm is perceivable.

name: Number Tug-of-War
topics_techniques_covered: balance_equivalence: keep the rope centered by making both teams' totals equal
quantitative_comparison: greater / less / equal
compare two magnitudes and judge greater / less / equal
number_sentence_building: enter values to make both sides equal
number_sense_magnitude
one_liner: Two teams of numbered characters pull a rope; the child taps the stronger side, or adds characters so the totals match and the flag stays centered.
interaction: A rope with a center flag stretches between two teams. Each character shows a number (its pull) and the total pull on each side moves the flag proportionally, so the bigger total drags the flag toward it. Two modes: (a) compare - the teams flash and the child taps the side that will win, or a center TIE button when equal; (b) balance - the child drags numbered characters onto a team (or into an empty slot) until both totals match and the flag locks at center. Submission = single tap (compare) or Lock at center (balance).
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the left team totals 5 and the right totals 3 so the flag slides left and the left team cheers; the hand then drags a 2 onto the right, the totals read 5 and 5, and the flag snaps to center with a chime. One unscored warm-up shows 2 versus 1 and the hand taps the stronger side. The flag's motion makes more-pull-wins and equal-pull-ties obvious wordlessly.

learning_science.principle: Analogue magnitude comparison (mental number line)
learning_science.why: Judging which of two quantities is greater draws on an analogue magnitude representation whose precision indexes numerical ability and is measurable before formal arithmetic, letting young children demonstrate quantitative reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scale the difference between the two team totals adaptively (a distance/ratio staircase) and credit accuracy-held speed on the tap-the-winner mode.
learning_science.source: Dehaene, Dupoux & Mehler (1990), 'Is numerical comparison digital? Analogical and symbolic effects in two-digit number comparison', Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance 16(3):626-641.

learning_science.principle: Central conceptual structure for number (compare and equalize)
learning_science.why: A mental-number-line central conceptual structure lets children coordinate comparison and equalization of quantities, the reasoning behind making two sides fair, and its development marks quantitative competence in the early grades.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include an equalize (make-it-fair) mode requiring the child to add exactly the difference to the smaller side, and score whether the first move targets that difference.
learning_science.source: Case & Okamoto (1996), 'The role of central conceptual structures in the development of children's thought', Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development 61(1-2).

tail_precision_rationale: On the speeded compare mode the joint speed-accuracy operating point and false-alarm rate separate careful-fast (able) responders from impulsive fast-wrong ones so raw speed is never rewarded; on the balance mode revisions and whether the first move equals the exact difference reveal direct computation versus trial and error, adding process variance beyond correctness at the cut.
age_rationale: Tapping the stronger team is a K-1-level judgement and adding one character to make a tie is within K-1 counting; totals, team sizes, number formats, and the closeness of the two totals escalate for older bands, and 6-8 can face multi-member sums and fractions. The tap/drag interaction is constant, reading is removed, and K-8 marks one shell spanning the whole range via adaptive closeness.

adaptive.content_range: compare and equalize within 10 with obvious differences (K-1) through multi-member two-digit or fractional totals with near-equal sides (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: total magnitude, closeness of the two totals (distance/ratio), number of members per team, integer vs fractional pulls, compare vs equalize mode, and flashed-then-masked vs static
adaptive.notes: Teams are generated from target totals with a computed difference; the closeness staircase feeds M-SPEEDACC and the equalize target feeds first-move scoring.

engagement_hook: A lively rope that lurches toward the stronger team and a flag that snaps to center on a perfect tie make comparison and equalizing feel like refereeing a playground contest.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Speed pressure inducing impulsive taps (credit only accuracy-held speed and log M-FALSEALARM; anticipatory taps under a floor are discounted); motor load (large team drop zones, single-tap compare); reading removed via numerals and icons; flag position readable by displacement and a center line, not color alone; keep TIE equally reachable to avoid position bias.

name: Number Grid Lock
topics_techniques_covered: numeric_matrix: find the missing number that satisfies a matrix of relations
number_analogies: infer the quantitative relation in a 2x2 and complete it
number_series
Number Series: determine the missing number in a sequence
quantitative_reasoning_mixed: verbal and nonverbal number problems and patterns
one_liner: The child cracks a numeric safe by dialing the missing number(s) so every row and column of the grid satisfies its hidden relation.
interaction: A safe's dial-grid shows numbers with one (or more) blank cell. Each row and each column follows a relation (a constant step, a sum, or a multiply). The child selects a blank and dials its value with plus/minus wheels or taps a candidate; a row or column clicks and lights when its relation is satisfied, and the lock opens when all lines hold. A K-1 entry uses a single row (a counting/skip series); 2x2 grids introduce a cross relation (analogy); 3x3 grids require row and column relations at once. Submission = Open (commit) once the cells are set.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): a 2x2 shows 2,4 over 3,? with a glowing x2 arrow across the top row; the hand dials the bottom-right to 6 so the column and row both click and the lock pops open with a chime. One unscored warm-up is a single row 1,2,3,? dialed to 4. The clicking lines teach make-every-line's-pattern-true without words.

learning_science.principle: Component processes of analogical and relational inference
learning_science.why: Solving a numeric analogy or matrix requires encoding elements, inferring the relation, and mapping and applying it - separable reasoning components whose demand marks higher quantitative reasoning distinct from calculation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Design distractors so each foil satisfies some but not all relations, so the chosen value reveals which relational components the child applied, and tag errors to the missed relation.
learning_science.source: Sternberg (1977), 'Component processes in analogical reasoning', Psychological Review 84(4):353-378.

learning_science.principle: Rule abstraction and goal management in matrices
learning_science.why: Matrix-reasoning ability is driven by the number of relational rules a solver can induce and manage toward the goal cell simultaneously, which is a strong marker of fluid and quantitative reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scale the number of co-acting row/column rules and record the maximum simultaneously satisfied rules on correct high-complexity locks (rule dimensionality).
learning_science.source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990), 'What one intelligence test measures: A theoretical account of the processing in the Raven Progressive Matrices Test', Psychological Review 97(3):404-431.

tail_precision_rationale: Rule dimensionality solved (M-RULEID) exposes how many co-acting row/column relations a child binds at once - separating two correct children at 1 versus 3 simultaneous rules where a single difficulty index blurs them - while first-action latency indexes reflective encoding, hint-free solving is stronger evidence, and M-DIFFREACH over grid size and rule count pinpoints the relational ceiling that most sharply separates the upper tail.
age_rationale: The lock shell degrades gracefully to a single-row counting/skip series that K-1 can crack, becomes a 2x2 cross-relation (analogy) at 2-3, a 3x3 single-rule matrix at 4-5, and a 3x3 with two co-acting row/column rules and larger or fractional numbers at 6-8; dialing or tapping a cell is low motor and notation-free, and K-8 marks the one shell spanning counting series to relational matrices via adaptive complexity.

adaptive.content_range: single-row counting/skip series (K-1) through 3x3 two-rule numeric matrices with larger or fractional entries (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size (1 row to 3x3), number of co-acting rules, relation type (additive/multiplicative/mixed), number of blanks, number magnitude/format, and candidate-tap vs free-dial entry
adaptive.notes: Grids are generated by sampling row/column relations then blanking cells; foils are keyed to individual missed relations for M-RULEID and error typing, and grid size and rule count set M-DIFFREACH.

engagement_hook: Each satisfied row or column clicks like a safe tumbler and the lock springs open when every line is true, turning numeric-matrix and series reasoning into cracking a vault.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Dial/keypad motor and numeral load (offer candidate-tap for young bands); trial-and-error dialing using the click cues (captured via M-RTFIRST, M-HINT and commit-blind locks in the bank); no reading required (numerals and iconic relation arrows); the satisfied-line cue is shown by a lit outline and a click, not color alone; cap magnitudes so the relation, not computation, is the bottleneck.

name: Quantitative Reasoning Quest
topics_techniques_covered: quantitative_reasoning_mixed: verbal and nonverbal number problems and patterns
number_series
numeric_matrix
balance_equivalence
quantitative_comparison
word_problem_reasoning
proportional_reasoning
one_liner: The child travels a quest map where each gate is a short number challenge in a different format - compare, series, matrix, balance, ratio, or a pictured story - routed to stay at the edge of what they can do.
interaction: An avatar advances along a path of gates. Each gate poses one bite-size item drawn from a rotating set of formats: tap-the-greater (comparison), tap the next term (series), dial the missing cell (matrix), pick the weight that balances (equivalence), pick the equal ratio (proportion), or solve a pictured/audio one-step story (word problem). The child answers with a single tap or a dial; a correct answer advances the avatar and steps difficulty up, a miss steps difficulty down (adaptive routing). Some gates are matched clones of an earlier format to check consistency. Submission = per-gate tap/confirm; the run ends after a fixed number of gates or at a stable ceiling.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the avatar reaches a compare gate and the hand taps the bigger of two groups to open it and step forward, then a series gate opens by tapping the next number; each format shows its own tiny ghost-hand the first time it appears. One unscored warm-up gate (compare 2 vs 5) starts the run. Because every gate reuses the wordless conventions of the single-format types, each new format self-teaches in one animated beat.

learning_science.principle: Adaptive (tailored) testing for tail precision
learning_science.why: Routing each item to the child's current ability holds measurement near the person's edge, which minimizes the standard error exactly at the high cut where fixed forms are least informative.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Step difficulty up on success and down on failure across a wide above-level bank so the run converges on the child's ceiling with few items.
learning_science.source: Weiss (1982), 'Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing', Applied Psychological Measurement 6(4):473-492.

learning_science.principle: Interleaving of mixed problem types
learning_science.why: Interleaving different problem formats forces the solver to identify which kind of reasoning each item needs, discriminating flexible quantitative reasoners from those who only pattern-match a single practiced format.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Randomly interleave formats rather than blocking them, and log per-format accuracy to profile breadth versus a narrow spike.
learning_science.source: Rohrer & Taylor (2007), 'The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning', Instructional Science 35(6):481-498.

tail_precision_rationale: Adaptive routing drives M-DIFFREACH (the ceiling reached across formats) as the sharpest single tail statistic, while cross-format consistency (M-CONSIST) on interleaved matched clones lowers the conditional standard error near the cut and flags spiky single-format performers; the progress trajectory (M-PROG) and end-of-run drift (M-DRIFT) turn one longer session into a curve and gate the decision on sustained engagement rather than a fatigued tail.
age_rationale: The quest starts every child at easy, K-1-appropriate gates (compare, count-on) and routes upward, so the same shell serves all bands; the hardest gates (multi-rule matrices, proportional and multi-step story gates) only appear for children who climb to them, so no band faces items beyond its reach. The single-tap/dial answers are low motor and reading is removed by spoken plus pictured gates, and K-8 marks the deliberately full-range adaptive span.

adaptive.content_range: count/compare gates (K-1) through multi-rule matrix, proportional, and multi-step story gates (6-8), blended and adaptively routed
adaptive.difficulty_levers: the per-format difficulty levers of each embedded format, plus routing step size, format mix, and clone-consistency rate
adaptive.notes: Gates are generated by the same parametric families as the single-format types; interleaving and the up/down routing are configuration, and matched clones across the run feed M-CONSIST.

engagement_hook: A quest where every gate is a fresh little puzzle and the avatar keeps climbing toward tougher challenges makes a full quantitative-reasoning battery feel like leveling up through a game world.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Format novelty and game-familiarity variance (each format keeps its wordless ghost-hand and an unscored first appearance); reading removed via spoken plus pictured gates; motor kept to a single tap or dial; adaptive routing must not trap a child in one format (enforce a minimum format spread); engagement and fatigue are monitored via M-DRIFT so late low-effort gates are down-weighted rather than scored as ability.

name: Number Analogy Bridge
topics_techniques_covered: number_analogies
number_analogies: infer the quantitative relation in A:B and apply it to complete C:?
quantitative_reasoning_mixed
one_liner: A child sees A goes to B and works out the same numeric relation to complete C goes to what, with an optional 'show how' bridge that animates the relation on concrete quantities.
interaction: The screen shows A:B :: C:? with each number also drawn as dots. The child may tap 'Show how' to reveal the relation label (for example x2 or +3) applied on the bridge, then taps the option that completes C by the same relation. Distractors are keyed to specific misconceptions (additive-instead-of-multiplicative, off-by-one, copy-the-source). The engine logs accuracy, which relational rules were integrated, response time, the misconception lure chosen, partial credit, and the hardest relation solved. Numbers are read aloud; no typing.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand (<=10s) taps 'Show how', the bridge animates 2 becoming 4 (doubling) with dots, and the same relation is applied to C to pick the answer with a chime - so the map-the-relation idea is obvious. One unscored warm-up analogy runs before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Analogical reasoning decomposes into inferring, mapping, and applying a relation (componential theory)
learning_science.why: A:B::C:? isolates relational reasoning - a core fluid/quantitative ability - and the componential view shows where children succeed or fail, letting distractors target the mapping step
learning_science.concrete_decision: Build items as an explicit relation to infer and apply, with distractors keyed to each componential failure so M-ERRTYPE reveals the breakdown
learning_science.source: Sternberg, R. J. (1977). Component processes in analogical reasoning. Psychological Review, 84(4), 353-378.

learning_science.principle: Relational complexity (the number of relations bound at once) sets reasoning difficulty
learning_science.why: Two-rule number analogies (e.g., x2 then +1) demand binding more relations simultaneously, a principled difficulty lever that separates the tail
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scale difficulty by the count of co-acting relations and score the maximum simultaneously integrated (M-RULEID)
learning_science.source: Halford, G. S., Wilson, W. H., & Phillips, S. (1998). Processing capacity defined by relational complexity: Implications for comparative, developmental, and cognitive psychology. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 21(6), 803-831.

learning_science.principle: Concrete dot representations lower the notation barrier to relational reasoning
learning_science.why: Drawing each number as dots lets young children infer a multiplicative or additive relation without symbolic fluency, broadening who can demonstrate the ability
learning_science.concrete_decision: Render every term as both a numeral and a dot set and offer an optional visual bridge so the relation is graspable across K-8
learning_science.source: Richland, L. E., Morrison, R. G., & Holyoak, K. J. (2006). Children's development of analogical reasoning: Insights from scene analogy problems. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 94(3), 249-273.

tail_precision_rationale: M-RULEID exposes whether a correct answer integrated one or several co-acting relations, separating children a single difficulty index blurs, while M-ERRTYPE's additive-versus-multiplicative lure profile pinpoints the exact relational misconception behind an error. M-POLY extracts partial credit from near-relations and M-DIFFREACH tracks the hardest relation solved under escalation, together concentrating information at the tail without requiring algebra notation.
age_rationale: With dot support and read-aloud numbers, simple doubling or add-one analogies are graspable in K-1; 2-3 and 4-5 add larger numbers and mixed additive/multiplicative relations; 6-8 adds two-rule relations and non-integer scaling. The 'K-8' band marks the type as spanning the full range so it can represent the K-8 number-analogy item.

adaptive.content_range: single-relation doubling/add-one with dots (K-1) up to two-rule and non-integer scaling analogies (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Items are procedurally generated from a relation template with distractors auto-keyed to additive/off-by-one/copy misconceptions for a stable M-ERRTYPE taxonomy.

engagement_hook: The animated 'bridge' that shows one number transforming into another turns an abstract analogy into a satisfying visual puzzle to crack.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Read-aloud numbers and dot renderings remove reading and notation load; the optional bridge scaffolds the relation without giving the answer; a wordless demo plus warm-up control novelty; distractors are meaning-bearing so errors are diagnostic rather than random; multiple-choice caps the ceiling, mitigated by M-DIFFREACH escalation and two-rule items.
